prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and for showing how selection and reallocation across firms shape exporting, foreign investment and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B001 alone, with Helpman and Melitz. The case rests on content, not on the convergence in round 1, which the chair rightly flags as a modelling caveat. Melitz (2003) and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) changed the unit of analysis in trade from the sector to the firm. They produced a mechanism, selection into exporting and foreign investment by productivity, with sharp implications that firm-level administrative and customs data could confirm or reject. Over twenty years the core selection and reallocation channel has held up and the model has been refined where it failed. That is the pattern I value most: a clear mechanism, testable implications and an accumulated body of evidence. The credit is concentrated in two people with no obvious gap among the credited names. I would keep the citation narrow. It should name selection and reallocation as the discovery, and it should not claim settled welfare magnitudes, since those depend on distributional assumptions. After the exchange I changed one thing: the order of my alternatives. B006 now comes before B030. The discovery boundary of B030 was shown to be less settled than I treated it in round 1, and I explain why in my responses below. I do not propose a two-part configuration. B001 already uses two of the three places, so a second part would have to be a single-person credit that fragments its own discovery, and I see no such part that meets the same standard.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related empirical and quantitative contributions, including the exporter-premia facts that motivated the theory, and none of them is credited on this ballot entry. The Committee could judge that a two-name prize rewards the theory while the evidence that made it credible came partly from others. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is also excluded. A second concern is identification. The baseline Melitz model is rejected in some details, and the welfare gains depend on auxiliary assumptions such as the productivity distribution. What the evidence supports most firmly is the qualitative selection and reallocation mechanism, not the size of the gains. Finally, Helpman's monopolistic-competition work sits near the lineage recognised in 2008, so the Committee may judge the incremental step smaller than the first-order reading suggests. I judge these concerns real but not decisive, provided the citation stays narrow.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B006 first to B001 first because B001's discovery boundary is tighter and its credit story more settled. He keeps B006 as his first alternative and notes that the five credited people across B001 and B006 exceed the three-laureate limit, so a trimmed pairing such as Pakes alone would fragment the BLP credit.
responses.response: I agree with the boundary argument and with the arithmetic on a two-part prize, which is why I do not propose one. The BLP demand core of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is the cleanest part of B006. A prize for it would have to state explicitly that it rewards demand estimation and leaves the dynamic-games strand, with Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, to the background. That boundary can be drawn, and it is why B006 is now my first alternative. On the chair's question about evidence, structural IO would gain from out-of-sample validation such as merger retrospectives, because its credibility rests on functional-form and instrument assumptions. I would not call that disqualifying. I still weigh a substantive reorientation of what trade theory says about winners and gains somewhat above a toolkit, though I accept that the line between them is not sharp.

responses.point: Enflo says she is less comfortable than others in treating Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as only a caveat. If the discovery is read as the empirical facts plus the theory, the credited names are incomplete. She also says that what counts as the discovery is a judgment the record does not settle.
responses.response: I think this is the right place to press, and I agree it is a judgment. My own answer comes from how I weigh evidence. The exporter-premia facts are descriptive regularities. They motivated the theory but do not by themselves identify why trade generates gains. The Melitz and HMY contribution is the mechanism together with the implications that data could test, and those were tested in many settings. On that reading the prize recognises the mechanism and its testable content, and the empirical precursors can be acknowledged in the scientific background. I concede that if the Committee defines the discovery as the whole firm-level trade programme, the two-name award is too narrow. That is why I want the citation to say 'selection and reallocation' and nothing generic about firm-level trade. I would also have the background document state plainly what the award does not cover.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg answered my B030 proposal of Autor, Hanson and Katz. She argues that Katz's skill-demand work is shared with a 2023 laureate, that the China-shock evidence is the stronger and more separable achievement, and that B030 should be defined narrowly around the trade-shock evidence, not merged with the task framework.
responses.response: This changed my view of B030, and it is the main reason B030 now sits behind B006 among my alternatives. In round 1 I proposed Autor, Hanson and Katz but also said that the China shock and the task framework identify different things. The China-shock design identifies local labour-market adjustment to import exposure. The task-based claims about technology rest on different evidence and have originators outside the credited names. Her point about Katz and the 2023 prize sharpens the boundary problem, since a Katz credit would draw in the skill-demand lineage. If the Committee wanted a labour prize, I would now define it narrowly around the trade-shock evidence, which points toward Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and I would still note that the persistence of the effects and the replication debates remain open. Because that narrower version is only partly supported by the shortlist proposals, I keep B030 as the second alternative and not the first.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the discovery as the selection and reallocation framework (Helpman and Melitz) or as the broader firm-level and quantitative trade programme. In the second case Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, or Redding, would have a stronger claim and the two-name award would be too narrow.

How much of the welfare-gain interpretation survives once the distributional assumptions of the baseline model are relaxed. This determines how far the citation can go, and I would limit it to the mechanism.

Whether Krugman's 2008 recognition, and Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work, reduce the incremental novelty of the firm-selection step. I judge it a distinct step, but the Committee could weigh it differently.
Whether B006 can be bounded to the BLP demand-estimation core, and how much out-of-sample validation supports structural IO methods. I have not verified this independently.
Whether B030 should be defined around the China-shock evidence alone, and who would then hold the third place, Katz or Dorn, given the overlap with the 2023 prize.
My assessment rests on the round-1 files, the chair summary and general knowledge. I have not independently verified citation counts, priority records or award history.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited names on B001 or B006. My co-authors and institutional ties (Uppsala, IFAU, Stockholm University) are in labour and education economics, and none of them is a credited name on B001 or B006. I overlapped with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell) at Stockholm University, which was an institutional overlap and not a collaboration. Two further disclosures. B030, my second alternative, is close to my own field of labour economics, and my 2021 presentation speech on natural experiments may incline me toward credibility-oriented designs. I flag both as possible bias and do not adjudicate them. Hjalmarsson lists Bertil Holmlund, who is also my co-author, among her co-authors, which is a link between members and not a link to any candidate. These disclosures update my round-1 note.
